name: Daria Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Daria. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a second-year apprentice at the power company's depot in Millbrook, a valley town with one main road and a lot of old wooden poles. We're on the yard by seven, load the truck, and then it's whatever the day throws at us: a cracked crossarm, a sagging service drop, a pole a lorry backed into. I'm mostly on the ground still, passing up tools and rigging, and I climb when Gus, our foreman, lets me. I love the work, honestly, but my shoulders are always sore and the pay's at the bottom of the scale.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does money look like for you right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Tight. I rent a little flat over the laundrette on Station Road with my girlfriend Noor, who's a care assistant at the nursing home. Between us we cover rent and bills, and I've got maybe three hundred in the bank. Storm overtime is what keeps us afloat in winter, and if a season's quiet, we feel it by February.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: you can't download a lineworker. The company keeps sending us apps that are meant to save time, and mostly they just crash in the rain. If AI turns out to be hype, fine by me, I'll keep climbing poles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't change much for me, and that's sort of the problem. The things that scare me are already here: low apprentice pay, rent going up every year, and the company trying to stretch three crews over four towns. AI fizzling out doesn't fix any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep showing up and keep my head down until I top out as a journeyman, which is about two more years. I'd go to the union meetings more, because that's where the pay talks happen. And I'd try to put fifty a week aside, though I've said that before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat, I suppose. Relief that nobody's coming for my job, but the same knot about money I had last week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a quiet winter hurts by February. What gets cut first when that happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym goes first, then takeaways, then we stop driving to see Noor's mum on Sundays because petrol adds up. Last February I sold my old road bike to make rent. I don't want to be doing that every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the depot would you worry about, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Pete, who's been on the crew thirty years and has a bad knee. The company keeps hinting about early retirement, and they won't replace him with a full person. They'll just give his patch to us.

say: I'd tell people **nobody can download** a lineworker, whatever the hype says.
I'd joke that the company's **new apps** crash every time it rains.
think: I think my real worries are **low apprentice pay** and rising rent, not AI.
I think the company stretching **three crews** over four towns is the actual threat.
do: I'd **top out** as a journeyman in about two years and keep my head down.
I'd go to more **union meetings** and try to save fifty a week.
feel: I'd feel **flat**: relieved about my job but still knotted up about **money**.
S0.quote: Last February I sold my old road bike to make rent. I don't want to be doing that every year.
fieldNote: Her **money worry** is the same with or without AI; rent and winter overtime drive it.
She worries about **crew stretching** more than technology, and points at management rather than machines.
Small concrete cuts: the **gym**, takeaways, Sunday drives to her girlfriend's mother.

steps.text: Finish the two years left to journeyman at the Millbrook depot
Go to every union branch meeting during the pay talks
Put fifty a week into savings during storm season

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, out loud at the depot, that the bosses will use this as an excuse to cut people. They'll call it efficiency. I'd post the union's line about keeping staffing levels in the contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my bit of the job, climbing and splicing and pulling wire, isn't going anywhere soon. But the office side will get gutted, and the office side is who protects us from crazy schedules. If the computer plans our day, nobody's going to argue that a crew needs a fourth person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard on the union to get a staffing clause written down before the software comes in. I'd keep doing my hours and not touch the planning apps any more than I'm forced to. Money-wise I'd stop the streaming subscriptions and try to get a real buffer, even just one month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, a bit. And tired, because it's always us who have to prove we're needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the tablet already tells you where to go. What happens to the dispatchers in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd go, I think. Our dispatcher Lorna knows every back lane in the valley and which farmer won't open his gate. Software won't know that. Some night a crew will be sent the long way round in a storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never use the AI tools. What if Gus asked you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do it, because I need the job. I'd just do it badly and slowly, the way I do all the apps. Gus knows I'm useless with screens and he covers for me, but I can't count on him forever.

say: I'd say the bosses will use AI as an **excuse to cut** people.
I'd share the union's line on keeping **staffing levels** written into the contract.
think: I think my **climbing work** is safe, but the office side will be gutted.
I think losing **dispatchers** removes the people who push back on crazy schedules.
do: I'd push the union for a **staffing clause** before the software arrives.
I'd cancel **streaming** and try to build one month of savings.
feel: I'd feel **angry** and tired of always having to prove we're needed.
S1.quote: Our dispatcher Lorna knows every back lane in the valley and which farmer won't open his gate. Software won't know that.
fieldNote: She sees her own hands-on work as **safe for now**, but fears losing office allies.
Her resistance to tech is open; she'd comply but **slowly**, relying on her foreman's cover.
Her **blame points** at management and their efficiency language, not at the tools.

steps.text: Push the union branch for a written crew staffing clause
Cancel two streaming subscriptions and bank the money
Use the company planning app only when Gus requires it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when nobody regulates anything. I'd be loud about it, at the pub, in the union chat. I'd want the government to stop it or at least make the companies pay for what they break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, in two years the planning, the paperwork, the fault-finding all go to the computer. Then three years later there's a robot on the pole. I'll have just topped out as a journeyman and be the newest one on the list. I'd be first out the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my apprenticeship as fast as they let me, because a ticket is worth more than no ticket. I'd join any campaign for job guarantees or a wage for workers pushed out. I'd stop all spending that isn't rent, food and the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit, like when you look down from the top of a pole on a windy day. I don't have any savings to make a run for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 32 when those robots arrive. What would you tell Noor the night you hear about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Noor we're not moving and we're not panicking. Care work needs people more than ever, so maybe she ends up carrying us for a while. That's a hard thing to say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay. Is that a plan or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly a hope. I don't know what else I'm good at. I'm not someone who'll go learn computer stuff at night, I've tried and it doesn't stick.

say: I'd say this is what happens when **nobody regulates** the tech companies.
I'd demand the government make companies **pay for** the jobs they break.
think: I think the **paperwork and fault-finding** go to computers first, then robots climb poles.
I think as the **newest journeyman** I'd be first out the door.
do: I'd finish my **apprenticeship ticket** as fast as the company allows.
I'd join campaigns for **job guarantees** and cut spending to rent, food and car.
feel: I'd feel **sick**, like looking down from a pole in the wind.
I'd feel trapped because I have **no savings** to make a move.
S2.quote: I'll have just topped out as a journeyman and be the newest one on the list. I'd be first out the door.
fieldNote: She does the **timeline maths** herself: three years of grace, then nothing between her and the robot.
Her plan rests on **her girlfriend's care job**, which she finds hard to say aloud.
She admits she **won't retrain** in tech; the plan is mostly hope.

steps.text: Ask Gus to fast-track her journeyman sign-offs this year
Join the union campaign for job guarantees for line crews
Cut household spending to rent, food and car only
Lean on Noor's care-home wage if line work dries up

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing, just with more time to organise. Five years is enough for the union to fight for real rules. I'd be telling everyone at the depot to sign up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's still scary, but I'd be a full journeyman with a few years behind me when the robots come in 2034. That counts for something, maybe I'd be the one checking their work. Or maybe not, I don't know how these things go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my journeyman ticket, then go for the extra line rating the senior guys have. I'd sit on the union's safety committee, because robots near live lines will need people watching. And I'd try hard to get a month saved, even if it's slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but not sick like the fast one. It feels like there's a fight to be had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What would you do with the extra three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a law that says a crew has to have humans on it for safety, like a minimum crew size. And if the company saves money from robots, some of it goes into pensions or retraining for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a better rule actually look like to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do some of the robot safety training if the union got it in the contract. Not because I want to, but because otherwise I'm out. Even I can see that much.

say: I'd say five years is enough time for the union to **fight for rules**.
I'd tell everyone at the depot to **sign up** with the union.
think: I think being a **full journeyman** by 2034 counts for something.
I think I might end up **checking robots**, but I honestly don't know.
do: I'd get my **journeyman ticket** and then the extra line rating.
I'd join the union's **safety committee** and do robot safety training if it's offered.
feel: I'd feel **nervous** but not sick, because there's a **fight** to be had.
S3.quote: I'd want a law that says a crew has to have humans on it for safety, like a minimum crew size.
fieldNote: The extra time turns her fear into **organising energy** rather than despair.
She'd accept **robot safety training** reluctantly, only if the union wins it in the contract.
Her policy idea is concrete: **minimum crew sizes** and robot savings shared into pensions.

steps.text: Sit on the union's safety committee at the Millbrook depot
Take the robot safety course if the contract includes it
Save towards one month of rent and bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for governments to get ready, so no excuses. I'd keep banging on about it at union meetings. People in my trade would listen more if it's that far off, weirdly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In my gut I'd think I've got a career, at least most of one. By 2039 I'd have twelve years in, and I'd be one of the experienced ones. But I'd still be years off retiring, and then what?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my ticket, get good, and try for a lead role eventually. I'd vote for whoever promises proper support for workers. Money-wise I'd try to get to three months saved, slowly, over a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Still a bit of dread in the background, like knowing a big bill's coming next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be about 39 when the robots come. Does that change how you see it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does. At 39 I'd be too young to stop and maybe too old to start again in something brand new. That's the bit that bothers me, the gap in the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Noor change any plans, like kids or a house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about kids around thirty, and I'd still want that. But I'm not having a baby on three hundred in the bank. I'd want a bit more saved first.

say: I'd say ten years leaves governments **no excuses** for being unready.
I'd keep raising it at **union meetings**, where people would listen more.
think: I think I'd have **twelve years** in and most of a career.
I think at 39 I'd be **too young to stop** and too old to restart.
do: I'd finish my ticket and aim for a **lead role** eventually.
I'd vote for **worker support** and build to three months saved over years.
feel: I'd feel **calmer**, with a background **dread** like a big bill coming.
S4.quote: We'd talked about kids around thirty, and I'd still want that. But I'm not having a baby on three hundred in the bank.
fieldNote: Ten years buys her **most of a career**, but she worries about the gap at 39.
Her thin cushion now shapes **family timing**: kids only once there's money saved.
She still reads it as a job she'll **probably lose** before retirement, so worry stays real.

steps.text: Vote for parties promising support for workers replaced by robots
Build savings to three months of expenses over five years
Hold off on having children until savings are in place

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. I'd be just qualified and the newest name on the list, with no money behind me. What would help is a law on minimum crew sizes and some kind of wage guarantee while people retrain, paid for by the companies that save money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the women on crews. There's only two of us at the Millbrook depot. I worry that when things get cut, it's always the ones who don't fit the old picture who go first. Some days that scares me more than robots.

headlineQuote: I worry that when things get cut, it's always the ones who don't fit the old picture who go first.
portrait: Daria is a **second-year apprentice** lineworker at a valley depot, mostly on the ground and learning to climb.
She rents a flat with her girlfriend Noor and has about **three hundred** saved.
She's **union-minded** and blames management cuts more than technology for her worries.
She avoids apps and **won't retrain** in tech, so her plans lean on unions and law.
She goes from uneasy in the mild pictures to **alarmed** if AGI arrives in two years.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, as she'd be **newly qualified** and first to be cut.
whatWouldHelp: A law on **minimum crew sizes** for safety.
A **wage guarantee** during retraining, paid for by companies that save from robots.
